title: Entanglement distribution and quantum storage of more than 8000 modes over a metropolitan network
authors: Angelo Gelmini Rodriguez, Louis Nicolas, Théo Sanchez Mejia, Pavel Sekatski, Nicolas Brunner, Towsif Taher, Rob Thew, Philippe Goldner, Mikael Afzelius
abstract: Entanglement generation between telecommunication photons and matter is central to fibre-based quantum repeaters. Achieving practical communication rates requires multiplexing, which multimode quantum memories can provide. Rare-earth-ion ensembles offer large temporal multimode storage by exploiting the numerous spectral channels within their absorption spectrum. Here, we report on a quantum repeater node comprised of a $^{171}$Yb$^{3+}$:Y$_2$SiO$_5$ multimode quantum memory, featuring a 250 MHz bandwidth and a $76.6~μ\mathrm{s}$ lifetime, and a bandwidth-matched entangled photon-pair source. We introduce and validate a quantitative measure of the effective temporal mode capacity using a Schmidt decomposition. With this platform, we demonstrate entanglement between a telecom photon propagating through a 25.3 km fiber spool and a 979 nm photon stored for $125~μ\mathrm{s}$ across 16340 temporal modes. Finally, we report a field deployment distributing entanglement over 5.66 km through the Geneva metropolitan fibre network while storing 8235 modes for $63~μ\mathrm{s}$.
summary: This paper reports on a quantum repeater node using a multimode quantum memory ($	ext{Yb}^{3+}:	ext{Y}_2	ext{SiO}_5$) to overcome rate limitations in quantum communication. They successfully demonstrated the storage and distribution of entanglement across thousands of temporal modes over both laboratory fiber spools and a real metropolitan network link. This advances the feasibility of long-distance, high-capacity quantum networking.
main_problem: The primary challenge is achieving practical, high-rate entanglement distribution over metropolitan distances by overcoming rate limitations inherent in single-mode quantum memories.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated the distribution of entanglement across a 5.66 km metropolitan fiber link while storing and verifying correlations across 8235 temporal modes.
method: They utilized an Atomic Frequency Comb (AFC) quantum memory in a quantum repeater node setup, combining it with Spontaneous Parametric Down-Conversion (SPDC) sources and performing Bell tests to confirm entanglement preservation.
model_or_system: The platform uses a multimode quantum memory based on the $	ext{}^{171}	ext{Yb}^{3+}:	ext{Y}_2	ext{SiO}_5$ crystal. Entanglement is established between a telecom photon in the fiber and a stored signal photon, with mode capacity quantified via Schmidt decomposition.
key_observables: CHSH Bell parameter ($S > 2$), effective temporal mode capacity (up to 16340 modes), coincidence detection rates, and interference fringe visibility ($V$).
important_parameters: Memory bandwidth of $250	ext{ MHz}$, storage lifetime ($	ext{AFC}$) of $\sim 76.6\ \mu	ext{s}$, and metropolitan distribution distance up to $5.66	ext{ km}$.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the fair-sampling assumption for Bell nonlocality revelation, and there is a noted trade-off between coincidence rate and storage time due to memory efficiency decay.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the experimental setup involving SPDC sources, AFC memories, and detection systems. Specific panels show correlation peaks in joint detection histograms and the measurement of entanglement via Bell tests over varying fiber lengths.
paper_structure: The paper details the physical system (AFC memory + SPDC source), introduces quantitative measures like Schmidt decomposition for mode capacity, demonstrates broadband storage capabilities using fiber spools, and culminates in a field deployment test over a metropolitan network while verifying nonlocality via CHSH tests.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses scalability issues in quantum networking by demonstrating high-mode count entanglement distribution, which is crucial for realizing large-scale quantum repeaters beyond simple single-photon links.
